## Two performances, identical score

Two players can hit every written pitch and duration and still describe
completely different gestures. One clips each note to half its allotted time.
The other lets notes overlap, leans into the high point, and holds the next
arrival back by a hair. Your score fixes the events. Performance decides how
those events occupy the air.

*Articulation* covers how notes connect or separate. Dynamics shape amplitude
over time, and phrasing uses accent, timing and contour to group events into
larger motions. All three get much clearer when you hold the event data strict
and let several renderers interpret it. Your expressive choices stay visible as
policies, and stop being unexplained edits to the notes.

## One score, two renderers

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 82
use_synth :piano

score = [
  {note: :c4, start: 0, duration: 1},
  {note: :d4, start: 1, duration: 1},
  {note: :e4, start: 2, duration: 1},
  {note: :g4, start: 3, duration: 2},
  {note: :e4, start: 5, duration: 1},
  {note: :d4, start: 6, duration: 1},
  {note: :c4, start: 7, duration: 2}
]

define :play_events do |events, shaped|
  cursor = 0
  events.each_with_index do |event, index|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    high_point = event[:note] == :g4
    amp = shaped ? (0.55 + index * 0.05 + (high_point ? 0.2 : 0)) : 0.7
    ratio = shaped ? (high_point ? 1.05 : 0.82) : 0.5
    offset = shaped && index == 4 ? 0.08 : 0
    sleep offset
    play event[:note], sustain: event[:duration] * ratio,
      release: 0.08, amp: amp
    sleep event[:duration] - offset
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

play_events score, false
sleep 2
play_events score, true
```

The first renderer treats everything alike: one amplitude, and every sound
lasting half its nominal slot. The second grows toward G, lets that high point
ring, and holds the following E back slightly. Both read the same pitches and
the same score times. What changes is the grouping, not the tune.

Can you hear where the second version thinks the phrase peaks? Nothing in
`score` says. That decision lives entirely in the renderer.

## Push each policy until it breaks

1. Set the strict ratio to `1.05`. Every sounding note now runs past the next
   onset, so you get legato overlap without one event in `score` moving.
2. Move the accent from G to the final C. Now the loudest moment is the arrival
   instead of the melodic high point, and the phrase suddenly seems to have been
   heading somewhere else the whole time.
3. Raise the offset from `0.08` to `0.3`. A small hesitation turns into an
   obvious delay, and since the event still has to fit its score slot, there's
   less time left for it to sound.

## Score time and performance time are different variables

Every event uses the shared schema: `:note`, `:start`, `:duration`. Start fixes
an onset on the metric timeline, duration reserves a slot. The renderer decides
how much of that slot actually sounds, and how loudly. That's why staccato can
shorten a note without corrupting the bar total or shifting the next written
onset.

Expression, then, is a mapping from structural events to playback parameters.
The high-point rule takes emphasis from pitch, the crescendo takes it from
position in the phrase, and the offset singles out one arrival. Swap any policy
or stack them, and the source notes never move. Arguments about performance
become concrete enough to inspect and rerun.

A quantised rendering sounds rigid, though how much deviation helps depends on
style and on the size of the gesture. These two passes give you a comparison,
not a verdict that the shaped one wins. Ruby validates the program. Only
listening on your own system tells you whether eight hundredths of a beat is
perceptible, or whether the amplitude curve is pointed at the wrong note.

Amplitude is relative, which trips people up. Push every event to `0.9` and the
phrase gets louder without acquiring a high point. A crescendo reads as
direction because successive values form a slope; an accent reads as emphasis
because it contrasts with its neighbours. Two policies can hand one note the
same number and still build different shapes around it.

One design decision here is worth naming, because it's invisible until it bites.
This renderer sleeps through each full event slot, so a positive onset offset
eats into sounding time. A different renderer could preserve the note's duration
and push every later onset instead, which changes the whole timeline. Once score
time and performance time have separate variables, neither choice stays
implicit. Name your renderer or its fields so the timing policy is readable
without anyone reverse-engineering the sleeps.

## Three performances from one score

Add optional `:amp` and `:articulation` fields to some events, and teach
`play_events` to interpret `:staccato`, `:legato` and `:accent`, falling back to
renderer defaults when a field is missing. Produce a detached performance, a
fully legato one, and a phrase-shaped one.

Every pitch, start and duration stays exactly where it is. That constraint is
the exercise: if you find yourself wanting to edit the score, the thing you
actually want is another renderer policy. Compare the three by the kinds of
connection and emphasis they produce, and note which policy you'd reach for
first next time.
